extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and visual-story adaptors (authors, storyboard artists, people turning a 'movie in their head' into prose or visual formats)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for taking a vivid mental image, movie/script, or suite of emotions and turning it into readable prose or a visual storyboard while preserving the original spark. Covers drafting, revision, POV/tense choices, and concrete storyboard/shot-mapping techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose needs room to breathe / avoid micromanaging details
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prose needs room to breathe." Don't try to deliver every little twitch or exact micro-detail from the movie in your head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you try to deliver the exact experience you see in your head it will overwhelm people and ruin delivery; over-describing robs the reader of the opportunity to see it their own way and 'over crowds' the delivery. Anti-pattern: describing every facial twitch or minutiae. Scoring note: stronger prose selects crucial details rather than exhaustive micro-descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and work with your personal creative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Different people start from different places (some see a movie in their head; others start from a 'feel' or sound of words). Don't force another creator's process onto yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't visualize, learning to force visual thinking may be wasted effort; instead use the channel that works for you (emotion, sound, voice). Accept multiple valid workflows and develop the one that produces results for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ideas from execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Having ideas (a 'movie in your head') is different from being able to execute them into a deliverable experience—creative work is mostly about execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on turning the spark into a crafted thing; execution decisions determine whether the intended experience comes across. Anti-pattern: assuming raw ideas suffice without structured drafting and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a rough-draft 'dump' (10-year-old-boy / dessert-first) to capture excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: "10-year-old boy watches the movie" and "dessert first writing" — let the excitement pour onto the page in a messy draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the part that excites you first, dump every thrilling image or beat without editing, then clean it in revision. Examples: writing the climactic scene early; using an outline that is essentially a child's excited retelling. Scoring note: this preserves initial energy; later passes handle structure and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use revision to restore or refine the 'lightning'
rubrics_metrics.description: For some writers the 'lightning in a bottle' shows up in revisions rather than drafting—revisions are where you may 'put the lightning back in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drafting leaks the beauty, use revision to recapture emotional impact, rhythm, and voice. Anti-pattern: assuming the first draft must contain final magic; consider revision a primary creative stage for certain writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the right framework: POV, tense, and genre shape whether the idea will work
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a scene or idea only works when expressed in a different POV, tense, or overall framework; 'the bottle needs to be shaped right to catch the lightning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to change POV (e.g., third person to first), tense, or even the genre framing to let the core idea shine. Examples: moving a passage into a more immediate tense, reframing a premise as a tournament/shonen-style structure to access different emotional questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearticulate the core spark to rediscover what excited you
rubrics_metrics.description: Step back and describe your thing to somebody new—ask 'what was it that excited me about this story?' to reconnect with the central impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use articulation to identify the emotional or thematic core and guide revisions or reframing. Example: verbalizing the hook or the single image that drew you to the story to avoid losing it through familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When adapting scripts to visual formats, mark camera/shot details and emotional beats
rubrics_metrics.description: For storyboarding/visual adaptation: read the script, watch the 'movie in your head,' mark where the camera cuts, and write a detailed list of shots (camera size, foreground/background, character positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete process: annotate the script with imagined camera moves, create shot lists, pinpoint and star emotional moments. Anti-pattern: attempting to board directly from the script without an intermediate mapping step if you need it; some artists can, but many need 2–3 translations (script → imagined movie → shot list → boards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use influences and study craft across media
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from other creators and media (e.g., video essays on visual comedy or editing) to translate techniques into your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended study examples: Every Frame a Painting videos on Jackie Chan or Edgar Wright for visual/comedic technique. Apply lessons from film/animation to pacing, visual jokes, and editing in prose or storyboard work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture immediate or transient ideas quickly (write them down when they appear)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a moment or dialogue appears (even as you fall asleep) capture it immediately—otherwise the detail can be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tools to record snippets (notes, quick drafts) so transient but valuable images or lines are preserved for later development. Scoring note: projects that preserve and integrate these flashes often retain more original energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible about where the 'lightning' is caught — drafting vs revision varies by writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers catch the spark in drafting; others do it in revision. Both are valid—pick strategies that match how you work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether you are a 'dessert-first' drafter (capture scenes out of order) or a 'revision-lightning' worker (draft flat, then enliven in edits) and structure workflow accordingly. Anti-pattern: forcing your process to match another writer's timetable.
